title: Blessings all day
hook: a rabbi of the Talmud taught a hundred blessings a day, scattered through the ordinary hours

segments.voice: Yesterday, counting the Omer: seven weeks of days, counted aloud one by one. Your line was count the days. What did you begin counting, and what number are you on? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-five.

A hundred. That's the number a rabbi named. Rabbi Meir, the Talmud says, taught that a person is obliged to say a hundred blessings every day. Not a hundred long prayers in a service. A hundred blessings: short sentences, scattered through the ordinary hours. On waking. Before bread. After washing the hands. On hearing thunder. A hundred sounds like a great deal, until you see how small each one is, and how many things in an ordinary day could be stopped for and noticed. Today is about that scattering.
screen: `A HUNDRED, SAID RABBI MEIR.` → `SHORT, AND SCATTERED.` → `WAKING, BREAD, THUNDER.`

segments.voice: A Jewish blessing, a beracha, has a shape people come to recognize. It opens by speaking to God directly, blessed are you, Lord our God, king of the universe, and then it names what's in front of the person: the one who brings bread from the earth, the one who creates the fruit of the vine. The Mishnah gives a whole chapter to blessings for things a person might meet. On seeing lightning, or hearing thunder. On seeing mountains, or the sea. On hearing good news, and on hearing bad news; there's a blessing for that too. The Talmud records a blessing for after using the bathroom, thanking God for a body made with openings that work as they should. Nothing is too ordinary to be noticed. Here's the idea underneath. A blessing comes before or alongside the thing, so it works like a small door. You don't just eat the apple. You stop for a moment, see that there is an apple, name where it came from, and then eat. The Talmud makes a striking claim about this. Whoever enjoys something of this world without a blessing, it says, is like someone who has taken what belongs to heaven. And the verse it leans on is from the Psalms, in the King James: "The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof." Read this way, a hundred blessings is less a quota than a way of walking through a day with the doors open. By evening, a person has stopped a hundred times to notice something given.
screen: `THE SHAPE OF A BLESSING.` · `THUNDER, MOUNTAINS, BAD NEWS.` · `A SMALL DOOR BEFORE THE THING.` · `ENJOYING WITHOUT A BLESSING.` · then, large: `THE EARTH IS THE LORD'S.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say five blessings, beginning right now. Settle, and breathe. Then look around slowly for five things: the chair under you, the air coming in, a sound from outside, your own hands, the light in the room. Stay with each one long enough to really see it. If you pray, you can use the old opening, blessed are you, and name the thing. If you don't, simply say a quiet thank you for it, inside. Five small stops. The bell holds the time.
Blessings all day. Short Jewish blessings, scattered through the ordinary hours, a hundred of them in Rabbi Meir's teaching. Today's word.

Your line: a hundred blessings. Today, aim for five: before you eat, when you step outside, when some news arrives, and two more you find on your own. Count them as you go. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Observant Jews say short blessings throughout the day, on waking, before and after eating, after using the bathroom, and on seeing or hearing things like thunder, the sea or good news, aiming for a hundred a day.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hundred blessings sounds like a very long prayer service.
what it means: short blessings scattered through an ordinary day, each one a small stop to notice what's been given.
what a scholar hears: Rabbi Meir's hundred in the Talmud, the Mishnah's blessings for thunder and bad news, and Psalm 24 behind the claim that unblessed enjoyment is a kind of taking.

notes: Menachot 43b: Rabbi Meir says a person is obligated to recite a hundred blessings every day; paraphrased.

The blessing formula (baruch atah Adonai Eloheinu melech ha-olam) and the endings for bread (hamotzi) and wine (borei pri hagafen) are described in English without quotation marks, as a description of a real blessing, not a new one. Confirm the rendering.
Mishnah Berakhot 9:1–2: blessings on lightning, thunder, mountains, seas, good news and bad news; summarized. Confirm.
Asher yatzar (Berakhot 60b) summarized as 'a body made with openings that work as they should'; confirm tone is appropriate.
Berakhot 35a: one who benefits from this world without a blessing is as if he misused consecrated property (me'ilah), derived from Psalm 24:1; paraphrased as 'taken what belongs to heaven'. Confirm.
howItsDone says observant Jews aim for a hundred a day; confirm wording.
